events.title: AWS Student Builder Group UCC Launch: Your Cloud Journey Starts Here
events.summary: The online launch of the group: who we are, the basics of cloud computing, and advice on getting started from guest speaker Isaac Tandoh.

review.notes: No end time in any source. endsAt equals startsAt, so the site shows the start time only. Body follows the recap (S6); the announced live Q&A is not claimed.

events.body:
## Day One

We launched the AWS Student Builder Group at University of Cape Coast on Google Meet, for students interested in cloud computing, AWS, DevOps and technology more widely. It was free, and no AWS experience was needed.

We introduced the group, explained why we were starting it and what students could expect, and shared the activities we had planned. Then we went through the fundamentals of cloud computing.

## Guest speaker

Isaac Tandoh, AWS Cloud Trainer and DevOps Engineer, talked about how cloud and AWS are used in industry, where DevOps fits, and how students can start learning. Matthew Ntsiful also joined us and shared some of his own experience and encouragement.

Our recap ended: "Day One is officially in the books. Now, we build!"

events.body:
## About the session

Our second event focused on turning an interest in cloud computing into a practical plan. We walked through the AWS certification pathway, from Foundational to Associate, Professional and Specialty, and discussed cloud roles open to students at different stages.

## Guest speaker

Nathaniel Agbenyenu: Senior DevOps Engineer, Cloud Security and FinOps Lead at IT Consortium, and Co-Lead of AWS User Group Accra.

## What we talked about

- AWS certifications and where they fit
- Career paths in cloud computing
- The skills that matter beyond certifications
- Opportunities for students who want to work in cloud

The point that stood out: certifications can be part of the path, but they are not the goal. Practical skills, experience and steady learning matter just as much. Nathaniel closed with a simple reminder: "We don't give up over here."

## About the session

An online welcome for the freshers who had just joined the group, and for any UCC student new to AWS or cloud computing. No experience was needed.

## What happened

We introduced the community, what we plan to do at UCC and the opportunities we are working on for students. Core team members Kelvin Opoku and Evans Opoku then took everyone through the fundamentals of cloud computing, using simple analogies and real-world examples.

## On the agenda

- What AWS is and what you can do with it
- Why cloud skills matter for students
- AWS certifications and career opportunities
- A short live demo on AWS
- Getting started with AWS Builder Center

From our recap: "You don't have to know everything before you start. What matters is your willingness to learn, practise, collaborate, and keep building."

events.body:
## About the session

From Code to Cloud was our first in-person build session, in the Computer Lab at the New Science Annex. The goal was to take a personal portfolio from a local folder to a live website on AWS, then connect it to an Amazon EC2 backend. We got into the lab half an hour late, at 10:00 AM, so we finished at 2:00 PM instead of 1:00 PM.

## What we did

- Joel Anarba Amuni, our group leader, introduced the group, and attendees signed up to AWS Builder Center with the group's invite link.
- Joel then covered what cloud computing and AWS are, the Europe (Ireland) Region, the two services for the day, Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2, and AWS account safety basics.
- Lab 1, led by Kelvin Opoku Boateng: participants added their own name, bio and projects to the starter portfolio, created an S3 bucket, uploaded the files, enabled static website hosting and opened their live link.
- Then we broke the sites on purpose. Kelvin triggered an Access Denied error, and the room read the error and fixed the bucket policy.
- Lab 2: participants launched an Amazon EC2 instance from a startup script, added its address to the site's config.js and re-uploaded it, so the visit counter and guestbook on their portfolio ran from their own server.
- A 20-question Wayground quiz over refreshments. The top three won group swag, to be handed over when it arrives.
- A group photo, and a reminder to terminate the EC2 instances so they stop running. The websites stay live.

posts.title: Our first website on Amazon S3
posts.excerpt: Week 3 of the Zero to Cloud Practitioner bootcamp took participants from compute and storage concepts to a working Hostel Finder website on Amazon S3, with configuration and bucket policy errors to work through on the way.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S1, S2 and S13. Session date Sat 31 Oct 2026 is derived from the post timestamp and photo filenames.

posts.body:
## From concepts to a working website

Week 3 of our Zero to Cloud Practitioner bootcamp was a chance to put what participants had been learning into practice.

We began with two areas of cloud computing: compute and storage. Using real-life examples, we looked at what each one means and the part it plays in the applications people use every day. An application needs computing resources to run, and its files and data need somewhere to be stored and read from. Once that is clear, many AWS services become easier to place.

Then came the practical session. Participants were guided through deploying a Hostel Finder website on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), with one objective: take a website and make it reachable over the internet using an AWS storage service. By the end of the exercise, every participant had deployed the website and made it publicly accessible.

For many participants, it connected what they had been learning about cloud services with something they could deploy and open themselves.

## Learning through the errors

Getting the website online was not entirely straightforward. Some participants ran into problems with configurations and bucket policies, and getting past them took troubleshooting, careful attention to settings and help from others in the room.

That was part of the lesson. Working with cloud services is more than following instructions and expecting everything to work on the first attempt. Reading an error, checking the configuration and working out what to change are practical cloud skills in their own right.

Participants helped one another understand what was going wrong and how to move forward, and in the end everyone reached the same result: a working Hostel Finder website on Amazon S3.

## A podium to finish

We wrapped up with a Kahoot quiz on topics from the first three weeks of the bootcamp: a chance to revisit what had been covered, test understanding and add some friendly competition.

Congratulations to everyone who made it onto the podium and took home some AWS swag.

## Next: more compute services

The following Saturday was set to go further into AWS compute services, with practical introductions to Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Lambda. Having deployed a website from storage, the next step was to look at other ways applications run on AWS: on virtual servers, and as serverless functions.

posts.title: Certifications are part of the path, not the goal
posts.excerpt: Notes from our second event, where Nathaniel Agbenyenu talked through AWS certifications, cloud career paths, and what it takes to build a career beyond passing exams.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S4 and S9. No attendance figure stated.

posts.body:
## The conversation

On Saturday 26 September 2026, we hosted our second event, Building Your AWS Career: Certifications, Career Paths & Opportunities, with Nathaniel Agbenyenu, Senior DevOps Engineer, Cloud Security and FinOps Lead at IT Consortium, and Co-Lead of AWS User Group Accra.

The session brought together students at different stages of learning cloud computing, around one question: how do you move from being interested in the cloud to building a practical career in it?

Nathaniel walked participants through the AWS certification pathway, from Foundational to Associate, Professional and Specialty. Drawing on his own work, he described the kinds of career opportunities in cloud computing and the skills employers look for beyond formal qualifications. He also pointed to learning resources and opportunities students can use as they build their knowledge of AWS.

We finished with a live question-and-answer session, where participants could put their questions directly to someone working in the industry.

## The point that stuck

The strongest takeaway was about keeping certifications in perspective.

An AWS certification is a valuable achievement. It gives you a structured way to learn cloud concepts, shows that you understand particular services, and lays a foundation for further professional development. But passing an exam does not on its own make someone ready to work in the industry.

Practical experience, the ability to solve problems and a willingness to keep learning matter just as much. That means going beyond exam preparation: experimenting with AWS services, working on projects, understanding how systems operate, and building the confidence to apply what you have learned. A certification is one part of a longer process of learning and professional development, not the final destination.

## The closing line

Nathaniel ended with a simple reminder:

> "We don't give up over here."

Progress in cloud computing takes consistency. There will be new concepts to understand, unfamiliar tools to work with and problems that need patience. What matters is staying committed and continuing to put what you learn into practice.

## What we are taking from it

Knowing the certification paths and the roles available is a useful first step. The real progress comes from what follows: exploring the technology, working on practical projects and practising consistently.

That is the kind of learning we want to encourage at AWS SBG UCC. Through conversations with people working in the industry, technical sessions and hands-on workshops, we hope to help students make better-informed decisions about their careers and find ways to put their knowledge into practice.

Thank you to Nathaniel Agbenyenu for sharing his time and experience with our community, and to everyone who joined the session and contributed to the conversation.

[See the event: Building Your AWS Career](/events/building-your-aws-career)

posts.title: The day AWS SBG UCC began
posts.excerpt: On 22 August 2026, we launched the group online with an introduction to cloud computing, a talk from guest speaker Isaac Tandoh, and a plan for a community open to students from every department.
posts.author: AWS Student Builder Group at UCC

review.notes: Expanded from detailed community notes supplied by Joel (24 Nov 2026) and sources S6, S7, S8 and S11. No attendance figure or end time stated.

posts.body:
## Our first gathering

On Saturday 22 August 2026, we officially launched the AWS Student Builder Group at the University of Cape Coast (AWS SBG UCC) in an online meeting on Google Meet.

The launch brought together students interested in cloud computing, AWS, DevOps and technology more broadly. For some, it was a first look at cloud computing. Others came to meet people with similar interests and hear what the group had planned.

We began by introducing AWS SBG UCC, the people behind it and what members could expect: opportunities to learn, gain practical experience, work on projects and connect with others who want to build with technology.

## Who the group is for

An important part of the introduction was explaining who the community is for. Cloud computing is often associated with Computer Science, Information Technology and software engineering, but students do not need to study any of those, or have a technical background, to start understanding the cloud.

Cloud technology supports services in finance, healthcare, education, agriculture, research, business, entertainment and many other areas. It is the infrastructure behind applications, data platforms and digital services that people and organisations rely on every day, so understanding how it works is increasingly relevant in many fields.

We want students across UCC to see how the cloud connects to their own studies and future careers. A business student can learn how cloud platforms support modern businesses. Someone interested in agriculture can explore how cloud infrastructure supports data collection, analysis and digital agricultural tools. Students in health, education, engineering and research can find where these technologies fit in their fields too.

That does not mean everyone has to become a cloud engineer. It means having the chance to understand the technology, see where it is useful and build skills that complement your own interests.

## Understanding cloud computing

After the introduction to the community and its core team, our Technical Lead took participants through the fundamentals of cloud computing.

Rather than assume everyone already understood the subject, the aim was a shared starting point: what cloud computing means, how it works and why it has become such an important part of modern technology. That goes beyond knowing how to use a particular AWS service. It means understanding how computing resources, storage, databases and networking can be accessed and combined to build and run applications.

## Learning from people in the field

One of the highlights of the launch was the session **Cloud and AWS in the Real World and Starting Your Cloud Journey**, led by our guest speaker, Isaac Tandoh, an AWS Cloud Trainer and DevOps Engineer.

Isaac connected the fundamentals to how cloud technology is used in professional work: the problems it helps solve, and how students can begin developing skills in the area. Drawing on his experience in cloud and DevOps, he gave participants a clearer picture of the opportunities in the field and of how to take the first steps.

Matthew Ntsiful also joined the conversation and shared some of his experience and encouragement with the community. Hearing how different people learned and now work with these technologies was an important part of the evening.

A question-and-answer segment followed, where participants asked the speakers about cloud computing and getting started.

We are grateful to Isaac Tandoh and Matthew Ntsiful for giving their time and sharing their experience at our first gathering.

## The community we want to build

We want AWS SBG UCC to be a place where beginners feel comfortable asking questions, experienced students share what they know, and members learn from one another across disciplines: exchanging ideas, experimenting with AWS services and working on practical projects together.

Nobody is expected to understand cloud computing before joining. Everyone starts somewhere, and we want the community to make that first step easier.

## What comes next

During the closing segment, we shared what members could look forward to and how to stay involved: practical learning, technical workshops, certification preparation, projects, and conversations with people who have experience in the industry. The aim is for members to move from hearing about cloud technology to understanding it, using it and building with it.

To everyone who attended, helped announce the launch or contributed behind the scenes, thank you for making our first gathering possible. We are especially grateful to our speakers and the core team.

If you are curious about cloud computing, AWS, software development, DevOps, or how technology connects to your own field, there is a place for you in this community, whatever your starting point or academic background.

Connect with AWS SBG UCC on [Meetup](https://www.meetup.com/aws-sbg-at-university-of-cape-coast), [WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/BnlWXQsAiJxBmZJwyYnpu0), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/awssbgucc), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/awssbgucc), and [X](https://x.com/awssbgucc), or [reach out on our contact page](/contact).
